steps_emergency.brief: What to say: what the door is doing (won't open, won't shut, dropped, went with a bang, hanging to one side, a cable loose), whether the car is in or out, and whether the garage has a door through to the house. What to do meanwhile, in plain words from the Table B and Table E rows: stop using the door, keep the motor off, never pull the release cord while the door is up, keep children and pets clear, and never touch a spring, a cable or the drum it winds on. The number from [CV: phone]. No promise of a reply or an arrival time unless [CV: response_time] is set.

faq_slots.question: Why has my garage door become so heavy to lift?
faq_slots.answer_brief: The springs carry the weight of the door, not the person or the motor; when one breaks or loses its tension the whole weight lands on whoever lifts it (Table B repairs: suddenly heavy, a spring has snapped; Table E springs). What to do until it is looked at, as things to avoid: using the door, running the motor, pulling the release cord with the door up. Spring work is specialist work (Table E): never a word on how to adjust, wind, release or replace a spring or cable. Then what a repair involves, from the Table A repairs stages.

faq_slots.question: Why does my garage door stop part way or go back up?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Use the assigned symptom's meaning and its linked local issue. Three genuinely different causes in plain words from Table B: something in the way of the safety beam or the door's edge, so the motor does its job and reverses; a roller, track or guide binding so the door cannot run; a motor whose travel limits are set wrong, so it stops short or will not meet the floor. Then what the local housing adds, then the fix from Table A, never a word on turning the motor's force up or bypassing a sensor.

faq_slots.question: Should I repair my garage door or replace it?
faq_slots.answer_brief: The honest test, from Table A repairs and Table B: a door whose panel and its frame are still good but whose springs, cables, rollers or lock have worn is repaired, because every one of those is a replaceable part. A steel panel rusted right through along the bottom edge, timber gone soft at the foot or where the frame stays wet, or a door bent so it cannot run square in its tracks is replaced, because no part puts that right. Say which is which; never push either way.

faq_slots.question: Can my existing garage door be made electric?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Often, and the door is checked before the motor is chosen: a motor moves a door the springs already balance, it does not lift a heavy one, so the door's condition and balance come first (Table A electric: the door's condition and compatibility surveyed before the drive is picked). What follows from Table A and Table E: the motor matched to the door, the safety devices fitted and tested on the fitted door, a way to open it by hand in a power cut, and the paperwork handed over. Never promise that any door can take a motor; a side hinged door is not assumed to (Table G). No figure, no brand unless [CV: materials_methods] gives it.

faq_slots.question: Will a replacement garage door need planning permission?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Point at the Table C and Table E planning rows and write what usually applies, with 'usually' or 'in most cases': a door of similar appearance in the same opening usually needs none; an estate condition that has taken the usual rights away, a conservation area or a listed house can change that; making the opening bigger, or turning the garage into a room, is different work with its own approvals. What the customer does about it only as the row gives it (check with the council where rights are removed). Never an Act's, an order's or a direction's name, never a figure.

cards.brief: A situation card, not a fault: the garage is a workshop, a gym or a utility room, or there is a bedroom over it or a door from it into the house, and the door is a single skin of steel with a draught round it and daylight under it (Table B insulated: a draught, daylight at the bottom, the garage still feels cold). cards.title: Heavy to lift, or won't stay up
cards.brief: Problem led: the door takes real effort to raise, drops back when let go, or went suddenly heavy after a bang from the garage (Table B up and over: heavy to lift, drops back; Table B repairs: suddenly heavy, a spring has snapped, a cable hanging loose). The one cause this card makes: the springs carry the door's weight, and one has broken or gone slack, so the weight is on whoever lifts it or on the motor. What the repair involves, from the Table A repairs stages: the fault found, the door secured, a matched spring or cable fitted, the door rebalanced and tested. Spring work is specialist work (Table E): the card never tells the reader how to adjust, wind, release or replace anything, and says only what to avoid: using the door, running the motor. Link the Garage door repairs page. On a plain page this is a planned repair with no promise of speed; the urgent framing belongs to the emergency variant.
cards.mechanism: a spring broken or gone slack, so the weight is on you

cards.title: Rusted through, rotten or twisted
cards.brief: Problem led, the replacement half of the honest repair or replace test: a steel panel rusted right through along the bottom edge, timber gone soft at the foot with the finish peeling and the wood swelling, a leaf rubbing or a panel scraping, a lock that will not line up because the door no longer sits square (Table B up and over, timber, sectional). The one cause this card makes: the door itself has failed, its panel, leaf or frame, where a repair only replaces parts. What replacing it involves from the Table A stages for the door type: the opening and its clearance surveyed, the old door out, the frame fixed, the new door hung, the gear fitted, the door balanced and tested. Say in the same breath that a sound door with worn springs, cables or rollers is repaired, not replaced (Table A repairs), and push neither. Never a judgement on the age or state of the doors in the area.
cards.mechanism: the door itself gone, not a part on it

cards.title: Nowhere to stand while the door opens
cards.brief: A situation card: a short drive that ends at the pavement, a car that has to be backed off the drive before the door will open, an opening the car only just clears, nowhere to stand when the door comes out. What decides it: how each kind of door moves, from Table E: an up and over travels outward as it opens and needs clearance in front; a sectional has no outward swing and runs back on tracks under the ceiling; a roller rolls up into a compact box over the opening and leaves the ceiling clear; a side hinged pair opens outward and lets a person in without lifting the whole door. And what the garage has above and beside the opening (Table A survey stages: headroom, guide positions, swing clearance). What the work gives them: the door type whose movement fits their drive and their garage, chosen after measuring, never the best door in general. No headroom or side room figure (Table G: none verified). Never that any door fits any garage. Link the door type page LINKABLE PAGES has.

problems.h2: When Your Garage Door Can't Wait

cards.title: A door that won't shut
cards.brief: The door stuck up or part open, the car and the tools in view from the road, and where the garage has a door through to the house, the house open too (Table B made to measure row: an unusable opening stays unsecured). The one cause this card makes: the gear that moves the door has failed, so nobody can bring it down and lock it. Table B names what goes: a hanging cable, a spring that has let go, a crooked door (repairs), a motor that will not stop at the floor (electric). Write the reader's situation, the reason it won't keep, and what usually happens when they call: the door brought down and secured by someone trained, never forced, then the repair planned once the part is known (Table A repairs: the fault found and isolated, the door secured). What the customer does meanwhile: stop using it, keep the motor off, keep clear. Never an arrival time, round the clock cover or a call out promise unless [CV: response_time] or [CV: emergency_callouts] confirms it. Never a break in figure.
cards.mechanism: nothing left holding the door down

cards.title: A bang from the garage, and now it won't lift
cards.brief: A loud bang, then a door that is suddenly heavy or will not move, a gap or a broken coil visible in the spring over the door or beside the track, a motor that hums and gives up (Table B repairs: a spring has snapped, suddenly heavy; Table E springs). The one cause this card makes: a spring has gone, so the door is out of balance and its full weight is loose. Why it can't wait: a door without its balance can move on its own (Table B: a failed counterweight allows uncontrolled movement, said in those plain words) and a motor run against it strains. What the customer does first: leave the door where it is, keep the motor off, never pull the release cord with the door up, keep children and pets away (Table E: spring work is specialist work). What usually happens: the door made safe, a matched spring fitted, the door rebalanced and tested (Table A repairs). Never a how to, never a word about pairs or sizes of spring the rows do not give.
cards.mechanism: a spring gone, leaving the door out of balance

cards.title: Hanging crooked or off its track
cards.brief: One side higher than the other, a cable hanging loose or wound off its drum, a roller out of the track, a door jammed part way with the car inside or out (Table B repairs: a cable hanging loose, the door crooked; Table B sectional: it sticks in the tracks, one side sits lower; Table B industrial: it comes off its track). The one cause this card makes: one side of the door is carrying its weight, so every move twists it further. Why it can't wait: using it worsens the damage and a door carried on one cable can drop or jam harder (Table B repairs skipped: continuing use worsens mechanical damage). What the customer does first: stop, do not force it, keep the motor off. What usually happens: the door made safe, the cable and drum or the roller and track put right, the door rebalanced and tested (Table A repairs). Never how to re seat a roller or rewind a cable.
cards.mechanism: one side carrying the door's weight

cards.title: What to do while you wait
cards.brief: What the customer can do before anyone arrives, in plain words from the Table B and Table E rows: leave the door where it is, switch the motor off at the wall or unplug it, never pull the red release cord while the door is up, keep children, pets and the car clear of the opening, and never touch the spring, the cable or the drum. Where the garage opens into the house, lock the inside door. If the car is trapped, say so on the call so the right parts come. The one cause this card makes: a door that has lost its balance can move without warning until it has been made safe. Never an instruction to prop, wedge, lift or patch the door; never a time by which anyone arrives unless [CV: response_time] is set.
cards.mechanism: a door that can move without warning until it is made safe

faq_slots.question: Can you get a stuck door shut on the first visit?
faq_slots.answer_brief: What usually happens: the door brought down and secured on the visit where that can be done safely, and the repair done there and then where the compatible part is to hand; where it is not, the door is left shut and secure and the part ordered (Table A repairs: parts availability varies). Never promise a same visit fix. No response time, no out of hours promise unless [CV: emergency_callouts] or [CV: response_time] gives it.

items.title: Measuring the opening and what's around it
items.brief: The survey stage from the trade facts: the width and height of the opening, the space above it and to each side, the swing room on the drive, the guide positions, the state of the frame; on a repair page, the fault found and isolated first. A part of the job, not a promise about the quote.

items.title: Choosing the door and how it will run
items.brief: The specifying stage from the trade facts: the door and its track arrangement, canopy or retractable gear, the leaf layout, manual or motor driven; the options from the Table A materials and methods cell or [CV: materials_methods], by their trade name. A brand or named product only from [CV: materials_methods].

items.title: Taking the old door out
items.brief: The removal stage from the trade facts: the old door, its frame and gear out of the opening. Where it goes only from the confirmed practices; otherwise say it is taken away or left as agreed.

items.title: Fixing the frame, tracks or guides
items.brief: The fixing stage from the trade facts: the frame fixed to the opening, the tracks, guides, barrel or hood fitted, named as the Table A row for this door names them. No figure unless the rows give one, and never a standard's number.

items.title: Hanging the door and fitting the gear
items.brief: The central stage from the trade facts: the sections assembled and hung, the panel hung and its gear fitted, the leaves hung and aligned, the springs, cables and seals fitted, named as the trade names it. On a repair page: the compatible part fitted.

items.title: Setting it up and testing it
items.brief: The balancing and testing stage from the trade facts: the door balanced, the travel limits and safety devices set, the operation and the release tested; on an electric page the safety performance tested on the fitted door (Table E: tested after fitting, not in a catalogue). Never a force figure or a test name.

items.title: Handing over and tidying up
items.brief: The last stage from the trade facts: the door shown working, instructions and the conformity or commissioning documents handed over where the row gives them, the opening and the drive left clear. What the customer sees when the job is done.

included.note: Fallback only: the tick items are the service's own Table A stages when the pack gives 6 or more; this set is used when it gives fewer (F-ITEMS-GENERIC).

cards.title: Sticking, scraping or stopping short
cards.brief: The things a homeowner notices first, from the Table B signs row for this service, in their words: it sticks in the tracks, the panel scrapes, the slats are bent, it stops before the floor, the leaves catch at the bottom. The one cause this card makes: the running gear (rollers, tracks, guides, hinges) worn or knocked out of line, so the door binds. Then what it leads to if left, from the skipped row: worn running parts impair travel, damaged guides stop it closing. What the job does about it from the Table A repairs stages: inspected, the compatible part fitted, realigned, tested. On an Industrial and commercial doors or Roller shutters page the card is the symptom in daily use (it drops or jerks, a safety edge is damaged, it does not stop when something is in the way, it comes off its track: Table B) and what a door out of use costs the business in plain words, no figure; the duty to keep a workplace door maintained said as what usually applies, never the regulation's name. Not a broken spring: the category page owns that.
cards.mechanism: rollers, tracks or guides worn or out of line

cards.title: Daylight, draughts and water under the door
cards.brief: A draught round the door, daylight at the bottom, a torn seal, the garage colder than it should be, water coming in at a joint (Table B insulated, sectional, timber). The one cause this card makes: the seals and the fit to the floor and frame have gone, so air and rain get past a door that is otherwise sound. What the job does from Table A: new perimeter and bottom seals, the floor and frame fit put right (Table B done badly: a poor floor or frame fit leaves gaps). On a Timber garage doors page the card reads as the finish peeling and the wood swelling, and the priming and finish coats the door's maker asks for after fitting (Table E timber finishing), never a product name the client values do not give. Never a U value, never a promise the garage will be warm (Table E: insulation on its own does not make it so).
cards.mechanism: seals and the fit to the floor and frame gone

cards.title: The motor works but the door doesn't
cards.brief: The remote lights up and nothing moves, the door reverses for no reason, it will not meet the floor, it cannot be opened in a power cut (Table B electric, roller). The one cause this card makes: something is stopping the motor, either its own safety devices doing their job (a beam broken, force met on the way down), travel limits set wrong, or a door that has lost its balance, which the motor was never built to lift. What the job does from Table A electric: the door's condition and balance checked, the limits set, the safety performance and the release tested on the fitted door. A power cut: the manual release, and an outside release where the garage has no other way in (Table E manual release). Never tell the reader to turn the force up, bypass a sensor or run the motor against a heavy door; never a spring instruction. Not the spring itself: the category page owns that.
cards.mechanism: a safety device, a limit or an unbalanced door stopping the motor

cards.title: A lock that won't line up
cards.brief: The lock misses, the bolt will not engage, the latch misses its keep, a leaf blows shut, the closer no longer shuts the door (Table B up and over, side hinged, personnel). The one cause this card makes: the door no longer hangs true in its frame (hinges dropped, stays failed, a frame moved), so the lock cannot meet. Then what it leads to if left, from the skipped row: a door that will not lock, or one that moves in the wind. What the job does from Table A: the door realigned, stays, hinges or closer adjusted, a new lock where the old one has gone. On a Personnel and side doors page where the door is the one between the garage and the house, say that a door that shuts itself and holds back fire usually applies there (Table C), with 'usually' and never the rating or the document's name. Never a security rating or grade for the door (Table E: the door type alone proves none).
cards.mechanism: a door no longer hanging true in its frame

cost.h2: What Affects the Cost of [SERVICE] in [CITY]

cards.title: The size of the opening
cards.brief: The size factor from the trade facts price row: a larger, unusual or non standard opening means a made to measure door; a large or heavily used opening on a commercial page. Say it plainly and give no figure.

cards.title: The door's specification
cards.brief: Insulated or glazed sections, timber or GRP against steel, a specialist finish, extra sealing, a security or fire rated specification where the page is a shutter or a personnel door (the trade facts price row for this service). A material only from the rows or [CV: materials_methods]; a brand only from [CV: materials_methods]. Code adds the price line from [CV: price_list] when there is one.

cards.title: Electric operation and its safety devices
cards.brief: A motor and the protective devices that go with it, a new electrical circuit where the garage has no supply, an outside release where the garage has no other door, more involved controls (the trade facts price row). Say why each adds to the job; no figure, no brand unless [CV: materials_methods] gives it.

cards.title: Work to the opening, and what has to come out
cards.brief: Repairs to the opening, a new frame, structural work where the opening changes, a low ceiling that needs a particular arrangement, a tight space to work in; on a repair page, more than one part gone, a part no longer made, damage to the tracks or frame (the trade facts price row). Say the business looks before it prices, from [CV: quote_method] only.

faq_slots.question: How much does [SERVICE_LOWER] cost in [CITY]?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Prices only from [CV: price_list]; otherwise how the quote is given, from [CV: quote_method] only. The four cost cards above already give what moves the price: name one factor at most, never the list again. Never a figure from memory.

faq_slots.question: How long does [SERVICE_LOWER] take?
faq_slots.answer_brief: From the trade facts timing cell only: the pack gives no standard duration for any door job (Table G), so say what decides it: whether the door is a stock size or made to measure (the maker's lead time, Table A), work to the opening or the frame, electric operation and its testing; on a repair page, whether the compatible part is to hand (Table A: parts availability varies). No figure. Nothing about when the job can start unless [CV: start_time] is set. This is the one place the timing is written.

faq_slots.question: Do you guarantee your [SERVICE_LOWER] work?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Start with yes, then the terms from [CV: guarantee_years] and [CV: guarantee_scope]: whether repairs are covered as well as new doors only as the scope says. A manufacturer's warranty only from [CV: manufacturer_warranty], said by part because the door, the motor and the finish carry different periods and a service record can be a condition (Table E). Described, never promised; never a number of years the client values do not give.

faq_slots.question: Are you insured for [SERVICE_LOWER]?
faq_slots.answer_brief: The cover figure from [CV: insurance_cover] and what the cover is for, with an example that does not suggest carelessness. Never what it pays or who it covers.

faq_slots.question: What happens if the door plays up after the work?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Open with what the customer does: tell us what the door is doing and we look at it. Then the reasonable care and skill standard every trade works to, as the standard the work is held to, never as a defence. No promise to come back free. Never invent a guarantee.

faq_slots.question: Do I need permission for [SERVICE_LOWER]?
faq_slots.answer_brief: From the trade facts rule rows only, put as what usually applies, with 'usually' or 'in most cases'. A door of similar appearance in the same opening usually needs no planning application; a listed house, a protected part of town or a condition on the estate that removed the usual rights can change that. Making the opening bigger is structural work the council usually wants to know about. A motor wired to a supply already in the garage is usually not notifiable; a new circuit from the fuse board usually is, or is done by a registered electrician. The door between the garage and the house usually has to shut itself and hold back fire. A front or entrance door is fitted by a registered installer or signed off by the council's inspectors. Never a standard's number, an Act's or a document's name, a figure or legal advice. Where the rows give no rule for the service, say no permission is usually needed for this work at a home and leave it there.

faq_slots.question: What does your [SERVICE_LOWER] service include?
faq_slots.answer_brief: The What's Included items said as a sentence, in other words: the measuring, the door and its gear, the old door out, the fitting, the setting up and testing, the handover. What it does not cover only from the services list, with one sibling service page or the category page linked; where the trade facts row says a repair and a replacement are different scopes, say so and link the other.

faq_symptom.frame: [SYMPTOM]: why does it happen, and what can be done?
faq_symptom.answer_brief: The symptom and its linked local issue, answered as asked. Name the part and the usual cause in plain words from Table B, what the local housing adds, what to avoid until it is looked at (never a spring or cable instruction, never turning a motor's force up), and what this service does about it from Table A. One figure at most.

cards.title: A short drive, or a tight opening
cards.brief: The customer's situation: the car has to be backed off the drive before the door will open, the drive ends at the pavement, the opening is one the car only just clears, or the ceiling is low. What decides it: how this door moves and what room that movement needs, from Table E and the Table A survey stages: a sectional rises and runs back on tracks under the ceiling with nothing coming out in front; a roller rolls up into a box over the opening and leaves the ceiling clear; a made to measure door suits an opening no stock size fits. What the work gives them: a door set back behind the brickwork so the opening stays as wide as it was built, and a car parked right up to it. Leads on the Sectional, Roller and Made to measure garage doors pages. No headroom or side room figure (Table G: none verified), never that any door fits any garage, never a fault invented for the old door.
cards.mechanism: how much room the door needs to move

cards.title: A garage you use as a room
cards.brief: The customer's situation: the garage is a gym, a workshop, a utility room or an office, there is a bedroom over it, or a door from it leads into the house. What decides it: whether the garage sits inside the heated part of the house, and whether the opening and the floor are sound enough to seal all the way round (Table A insulated: the intended thermal boundary surveyed, perimeter and bottom seals fitted). What the work gives them: an insulated door with its seals, and the honest line that the insulation in the door does not on its own make an unheated garage warm or airtight (Table E). Leads on the Insulated garage doors page, and on the Sectional and Roller pages where the insulated version is the one being chosen. Never a U value or a figure, never a heating bill claim, never a draught invented as the opener.
cards.mechanism: whether the garage sits inside the heated house

cards.title: Lifting the door by hand has had its day
cards.brief: The customer's situation: getting out of the car in the rain to open the door, a door that is heavy to lift, no side door into the garage, wanting to open it from the car or the phone. What decides it: whether the door they have is balanced and sound, because a motor moves a door the springs already carry and does not lift a heavy one (Table A electric: the door's condition and compatibility surveyed before the drive is chosen); the power supply (a motor on an existing supply against a new circuit, Table C, with 'usually' and no name); a second way in, because a garage with no other door usually needs a release that works from outside (Table E manual release). What the work gives them: a door that opens from the car, with the safety devices fitted and tested on the fitted door (Table E) and the paperwork handed over (Table A). Leads on the Electric garage doors page. Never promise any door can take a motor; a side hinged door is not assumed to (Table G); no brand unless [CV: materials_methods] gives it.
cards.mechanism: whether the door is balanced enough for a motor

cards.title: A door you walk through, not just drive through
cards.brief: The customer's situation: bikes, bins and the mower going in and out daily without lifting the whole door, a period house or a street where the doors match, a front door and a garage door the owner wants to go together. What decides it: the shape and size of the opening (Table A made to measure row: the dimensions and the structural opening surveyed first), what the material asks of the owner afterwards (a timber door primed and finished after fitting and refinished in time: Table E timber finishing, Table F), and for a front or entrance door the approvals that come with it (a registered installer or building control, Table C, with 'usually' and no name). What the work gives them: a pair of side hinged leaves that open outward so one leaf lets a person in (Table E), a personnel door beside the main door, a timber or made to measure door made for that opening, a front door fitted to the rules that apply, with an honest picture of the finishing a timber door needs. Leads on the Side hinged, Timber and Made to measure garage doors pages, the Personnel and side doors page and the Front and entrance doors page. Never a security rating or grade, never a brand, never a word about the look that the door's movement or material does not earn.
cards.mechanism: the shape of the opening and what the material asks of you

cards.title: The door's up and won't come down
cards.brief: The door stopped part way or stuck fully open, the car and the tools on show, and where the garage opens into the house, that door exposed too (Table B made to measure row: an unusable opening stays unsecured). The one cause this card makes: a cable come off its drum or a motor stopped mid travel, so the door is held where it stopped and nothing brings it down safely (Table B repairs, electric). Write the reader's situation, the reason it won't keep, and what usually happens when they call: the door brought down by hand by someone trained and secured, never forced, then the part replaced (Table A repairs: the fault isolated, the door secured, the compatible part fitted). What the customer does meanwhile: stop using it, keep the motor off, lock the inside door. Never an arrival time or a call out promise unless [CV: response_time] or [CV: emergency_callouts] confirms it. Never a break in figure.
cards.mechanism: a cable off its drum or a motor stopped mid travel

cards.title: A car trapped behind a door that won't lift
cards.brief: The door went with a bang and now will not move, or is suddenly far heavier than it was, with the car on the wrong side of it (Table B repairs: a spring has snapped, suddenly heavy; Table E springs). The one cause this card makes: the spring that carried the door has gone, so the door is dead weight with nothing to lift it. Why it can't wait: the weight is now on whoever tries, and a motor run against it strains and can damage the top panel. What the customer does first, from the rows: leave the door where it is, keep the motor off, never pull the release cord with the door up, never touch the spring or the cable, and say on the call that the car is inside so the right parts come. What usually happens: the door made safe, a matched spring fitted, the door rebalanced and tested (Table A repairs). Spring work is specialist work (Table E): never a how to.
cards.mechanism: the door's full weight with nothing left to lift it

cards.title: Off its track, or hanging on one side
cards.brief: One side higher than the other, a roller out of the track, a cable hanging loose, the door jammed at an angle (Table B repairs: a cable hanging loose, the door crooked; Table B sectional: one side sits lower; Table B industrial: it comes off its track). The one cause this card makes: a roller out of its track or a cable wound off, so the door is no longer carried evenly and every move twists it further. Why it can't wait: continuing to use it worsens the damage (Table B repairs skipped). What the customer does first: stop, do not force it, keep the motor off, keep clear. What usually happens: the door made safe, the roller and track or the cable and drum put right, the door rebalanced and tested (Table A repairs). Never how to re seat a roller or rewind a cable.
cards.mechanism: a roller out of its track or a cable wound off

cards.title: A motor that hums but nothing moves
cards.brief: The motor runs or hums, the chain or belt moves, the door stays where it is or lifts a little and drops back (Table B roller: the remote operates but it does not move; Table B electric). The one cause this card makes: the motor is straining against a door it was never built to lift, because the door's balance has gone or something is jammed in its path. Why it can't wait: every press wears the motor's gearing and can push the top panel out of shape, and a door without its balance can move on its own (Table B: a failed counterweight allows uncontrolled movement, said plainly). What the customer does first: stop pressing the button, switch the motor off at the wall or unplug it, never pull the release cord with the door up, keep clear. What usually happens: the door made safe, the cause found in the door before the motor is blamed, the part fitted, the door rebalanced, the motor's limits and safety devices tested (Table A repairs, Table A electric). Never a spring instruction, never a fix for the motor's settings.
cards.mechanism: the motor straining against a door it can't lift

cost.h2: What Moves the Price of an Emergency Call Out in [CITY]

cards.title: When you call
cards.brief: The time of day and the day of the week move the price: a door stuck open on a Saturday night against a weekday morning with a car trapped inside (Table A garage door repairs: urgent safety faults arise all year). A call out charge or an out of hours rate only from [CV: quote_call_out_fee] and [CV: price_list]; never say there is no charge for coming out unless [CV: quote_call_out_fee] says there is none. Whether the business comes out at those hours only from [CV: out_of_hours_available]; when it is not set, nothing about hours at all. Say it plainly and give no figure.

cards.title: Getting to the door
cards.brief: How far the garage is from the base, and what it takes to get a van and a ladder to it: a garage down a shared drive, a block of garages behind the houses, a car parked tight against the door, a rural lane (Table F garage door repairs: restricted access). Distance and access move the price; say why in plain words. Never an arrival time unless [CV: response_time] is set; never hours of cover unless [CV: out_of_hours_available] says so.

cards.title: Making the door safe
cards.brief: What is done first on a call out, from Table A garage door repairs: the fault found and isolated, the door and its gear inspected, then the door propped and secured so it cannot drop. What that takes moves the price: a door hanging on one side, a door that has come off its track, a spring under tension, a powered door with a safety fault (Table F garage door repairs: damage to tracks or frame, powered door safety faults; Table E: spring work is specialist). Never how it is done, and never anything for the customer to try on a spring or a cable. Say what decides it and give no figure.

cards.title: The part on the day
cards.brief: What has gone sets the rest: a spring, a cable, a roller or the gear against the motor, and whether more than one part has gone (Table F garage door repairs: multiple damaged components, specialist springs or obsolete parts). Common parts may be on the van, but a part has to suit that door (Table A: replacement parts must suit the specific door; parts availability varies), so whether it is still made matters. When the part has to be ordered the door is left secure, and the fitting follows as a second visit priced as its own job. On a door so old the part no longer exists, say so plainly; a new door is its own quote. A brand only from [CV: materials_methods]. Give no figure. Code adds the price line from [CV: price_list] when there is one.

steps.title: Call Us
steps.brief: What to say: what the door is doing (won't open, won't shut, dropped, went with a bang, hanging to one side, a cable loose), whether the car is in or out, whether the garage has a door through to the house. What to do meanwhile: stop using the door, keep the motor off, never pull the release cord while the door is up, never touch a spring or cable, keep clear. The number from [CV: phone]. No promise of a reply or an arrival time unless [CV: response_time] is set.

steps.title: We Make the Door Safe and Find What's Gone
steps.brief: The door secured first, then the fault found in the door before the motor is blamed (Table A repairs: the fault found and isolated, the door and its gear inspected); the customer shown what was found, photos only from the photos_of_faults practice. The price for making it safe agreed before any work starts only from the price_agreed_before_work practice and [CV: quote_method]. Never restates 'free'.

steps.title: We Agree the Repair and Do It Once It's Safe
steps.brief: The repair agreed and done on the visit where the compatible part is to hand, the door rebalanced and tested (Table A repairs); otherwise the door left shut and secure and a date agreed once the part arrives (Table A: parts availability varies). Never promise a same visit fix; 'same day' only when [CV: same_day_available] is yes. Never mention the price.

faq_slots.question: How much is an emergency [TRADE_PERSON] call out in [CITY]?
faq_slots.answer_brief: What moves the price, from the cost cards: the time of day and the day of the week, how far the garage is from the base, the access to the door, what making the door safe takes, and that a part that has to be ordered means a second visit priced as its own job (Table A repairs: parts availability varies). A call out charge or an out of hours rate only from [CV: quote_call_out_fee] and [CV: price_list]; the hours the business comes out only from [CV: out_of_hours_available]; an arrival time only from [CV: response_time]. How the price is reached only from [CV: quote_method]; the price agreed before work starts only from the price_agreed_before_work practice. No figure beyond what those values give.

faq_slots.question: How quickly can you get here?
faq_slots.answer_brief: From [CV: response_time] and [CV: start_time] only, as given; a same day visit only when [CV: same_day_available] is yes. Never '24/7' or 'any time' unless [CV: emergency_callouts] gives it in those words. This is the one place the timing is written.

faq_slots.question: Can you get my door shut and secure on the first visit?
faq_slots.answer_brief: What usually happens: the door brought down and secured on the visit where that can be done safely, and the repair done there and then where the compatible part is to hand; otherwise the door left shut and secure and the part ordered (Table A repairs: parts availability varies). Never promise a same visit fix. No response time, no out of hours promise unless [CV: emergency_callouts] or [CV: response_time] gives it. This is the one place the timing is written.

faq_slots.question: Are you insured for emergency [SERVICE_LOWER]?
faq_slots.answer_brief: The cover figure from [CV: insurance_cover] and what the cover is for, with an example that does not suggest carelessness. Never what it pays or who it covers.

faq_slots.question: What if the door fails again after an emergency repair?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Open with what the customer does: tell us and we look at it. Then that making a door safe is making it safe: the repair that follows is what the work is held to, under the reasonable care and skill standard, never as a defence. No promise to come back free. Never invent a guarantee.

faq_slots.question: What should I do before you arrive?
faq_slots.answer_brief: Leave the door where it is, switch the motor off at the wall or unplug it, never pull the release cord with the door up, keep children, pets and the car clear of the opening, never touch a spring, cable or drum, lock the door from the garage into the house where there is one, and say on the call whether the car is trapped (Table B, Table E springs). Never an instruction to prop, wedge, lift or patch the door. Whether the business deals with an insurer only from the client values.

faq_slots.question: Is this an emergency, or can it wait until a planned visit?
faq_slots.answer_brief: What counts as urgent for this service, from the card list and the Table B signs row: a door that will not shut, a snapped spring or cable, a door off its track or hanging to one side, a motor straining against a door that will not move, a car trapped. What usually waits for a planned repair, from the Table B rows: a noisy door, a remote that works some of the time, a worn bottom seal, a door that is slow but still runs true. Link the planned sibling page or the category page. Planned work is never dressed up as urgent.

cards.title: Garages built for the cars of their day
cards.brief: Rows of single garages on the estates the town profile dates, with openings cut for the cars of the time and up and over doors on most of them. The one cause this card makes: openings sized for smaller cars than people drive now, so today's car only just clears the frame. Tie the era to what the work involves, never to the state of anyone's door: the opening measured before a door is chosen (Table A survey stages), a door set back behind the brickwork so the full width is kept, a made to measure size where no stock door fits (Table F). Never 'the original doors are still fitted', never a judgement on the town's doors, never a figure for the opening.
cards.mechanism: openings sized for smaller cars than today's

cards.title: Integral garages under the bedrooms
cards.brief: The newer streets the profile gives, built with the garage inside the house, a bedroom over it and a door from it into the hall. The one cause this card makes: a garage that is part of the heated house, so its door is part of the house's outer skin. What that means for the work, in plain words: insulation and seals all the way round count for more (Table A insulated), the lock counts for more, and the door from the garage into the house usually has to shut itself and hold back fire (Table C, 'usually', never the rating or the document's name). Never a security rating or grade, never an invented break in figure, never that the door's insulation alone makes the garage warm (Table E).
cards.mechanism: a garage that is part of the heated house

cards.title: Short drives onto the pavement
cards.brief: Drives the length of a car, or less, that end at the footpath, and drives that slope down to the garage, where the profile gives the street layout. The one cause this card makes: the length and fall of the drive, which decides how a door may move and how its bottom seal meets the floor. What it means for the work: a short drive favours a door that goes straight up or rolls up, because an up and over travels outward as it opens (Table E); a floor that is not level needs more sealing work at the bottom of the door (Table F insulated: a level floor costs less). Never a figure, never that any door fits any drive. Not the door type choice itself: the service pages own that.
cards.mechanism: the length and fall of the drive

cards.title: Salt air and exposed sites
cards.brief: Only where the town profile gives the coast, an estuary or open high ground: salt and wind working on steel, tracks and finishes, a door that grinds or sticks sooner than it would inland (Table B: it makes a grinding noise, it sticks in the tracks). The one cause this card makes: weather getting at steel, tracks and finishes. What it means for the work: the finish and material chosen with the exposure in mind, only from the Table A materials cells and [CV: materials_methods], and a timber door's finishing kept up as its maker asks (Table E timber finishing). Where the profile gives no exposure, the card reads instead as the lock up garages in blocks behind the terraces, where the garage is away from the house and the door is left unattended, and what that means for the lock and for getting the old door away. Never a lifespan figure (Table G), never a brand.
cards.mechanism: weather getting at steel, tracks and finishes

cost.h2: What Affects the Cost of [WORK] Work in [TOWN]

cards.title: Getting to the garage
cards.brief: A garage down a lane behind the terraces, in a block of lock ups, up a shared drive or where there is nowhere to park a van: the door and the old one out are carried further and the work takes longer (Table F: restricted access). The profile says which streets. No figure.

cards.title: Openings that aren't a standard size
cards.brief: Where the housing era the profile gives left openings off today's stock sizes, the door is made to measure and the maker's lead time applies (Table F, and the Table A made to measure row). Say it plainly; no figure; never a judgement on the garages.

cards.title: Conservation areas and listed houses
